speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Mr. H. C. HOCKEN (Toronto West Centre):
speechtext:
I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) and in doing so to read an extract from a magazine called The American Mercury, published in Boston and edited by H. L. Mencken. In an editorial of the issue for June the following reflection will be found:
The average Englishman is a dull fellow and seldom shows any enterprise, but he knows how to follow leaders who have what he lacks, and he did it to immense effect for many centuries. But to-day, it must be obvious, there are few leaders for him to follow, and most of the few are pathetically fourth rate. It would be a sheer impossibility to imagine Palmerston or Disraeli swindled and made a spectacle of as Austen Chamberlain was at Geneva. It would be equally impossible to imagine the England of the great days following such dubs as Baldwin, Asquith and Winston Churchill-half of them fanatics and the other half rogues. The one English statesman who has shown any genuine skill at his trade for a generation past is Lloyd George, a petty attorney from a Welsh country town-the sort of fellow who, a century ago, would have served his country by sitting to Dickens or Thackeray, not by bossing the state. Nor has luck run with the Motherland on the next 'higher level. The amiable George V is so plainly a blob that alluding to the fact becomes a sort of cruelty, and his heir, searching the empire for a horse that won't throw him, becomes simply a comic character, even to the English. More and more they miss the waspish but hard-headed Victoria, and on blue days they miss dear Albert too.

desire to direct to the ministry a question based on an incident that occurred in this House on June 9. Mr. Speaker, it had been my intention to make the same request of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning), but as it has been preferred by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), I shall simply endorse his request.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, I am of course in the hands of the House in regard to the matter. I was quite ready to proceed to give any information desired by members of the committee with respect to the Welland canal item, but from all quarters of the House came cries of "Carried. ' and I thought the item was carried. In addition to that, another item dealing with the Welland canal was called, and I believe carried also. But if there is an opportunity under the rules of the House again to get into a position where I can give any information which any hon. member desires with regard to the Welland canal, I shall be happy to do so. I do not know how under the rules the matter may be revived, but I have certainly no objection to giving the information.

I would ask again whether the minister would place on Hansard an explanation with regard to this vote. The House is entitled to the information. The item only carried, I am convinced, on a misunderstanding. The minister, we assumed, was going to make a statement, but that statement was not made.

I am not just positive how a matter of this kind can be dealt with under the rules, but on the next occasion when the estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals come up for consideration in committee of Supply, I shall be pleased, with the consent- of the House, to give the information, and in that way it can go on Hansard, as welt as any discussion relating to it. I merely want to assure my hon. friends that I have no intention of avoiding a discussion with regard to the matter.

Mr. LAWRENCE A. WILSON (Vaudreuil-Soulanges) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker. I
would ask my colleagues of the French language to bear once more with me, while I express myself in the language of the majority of this House, in order to make a few remarks in connection with the bill at present before the House.
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of making some suggestions to the Minister of Finance. I shall be very cautious this time. When I made my maiden speech the other day I had had no acquaintance with Hansard. I find that the debates reporters are not only very capable stenographers, expert stenographers, but are really photographers because I think that every move I made on the occasion referred to was noted in Hansard.
Was your speech illustrated?

It
was rather in the nature of a cartoon. My purpose in rising on the present occasion is to help the Minister of Finance to increase the

Special War Revenue Act
revenue and thereby reduce taxation. I have the pretension to think that if my suggestions are accepted by the House they will result in increasing the revenue of this country by $20,000,000 per annum.
Hear, hear.

distilleries at 46 and 50 degrees under proof, given a preference over the imported of $6.20 and $8 per case respectively.
Is it fair to the Canadian government and to the people? No other country in the world has such an anomaly. To my mind the government should enact a law that no liquor in bottles, imported or domestic, should be allowed to be bottled or sold less than 25 degrees under proof and, in order to protect our distillers, the government should increase the customs duty to $2 per gallon, and leave the excise as it is at present. The government would reap a much larger revenue from both the foreign and Canadian distilleries and, at the same time, protect our home industries, which is only right, but, conditionally, that the strength be as indicated.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to that wonderful two-year law-a standing joke for many, many years. The excise law states that Canadian spirits must be kept in bond for maturing purposes at least two years before being offered for sale, but it fails to state that the spirits must be aged in oak or wooden casks. This is the little joker and the laughing stock of the foreign distillers or those who know. The great bulk of spirits, actually over 10,000.000 gallons, held in bond by the Canadian distilleries is kept in huge copper tanks or steel barrels where no perceptible evaporation is possible.
Would the hon. member allow me to ask him a question?
With pleasure. Mr. POULIOT (Translation): On what date was the order in council just mentioned passed?
That order in council dates back to Alexander Mackenzie's time. It is very, very old.
It has whiskers.

I must say, in justice, that I know of some distilleries that do age a portion of their output in wood, I have seen hundreds of barrels in Messrs. Walkers' warehouse, and I hope they reserve a fair portion for their friends in Canada.
Spirits cannot improve in copper tanks-
Hear, hear.

How about
human tanks?

Well, we pour it down the sewer. Spirits cannot improve in copper tanks any more than whiskey can improve in bottles, even if kept a hundred years. In

these receptacles there is consequently no evaporation of fusel-oil and such whiskey should not be permitted for consumption.
Notwithstanding this, the law allows these distilleries 17 per cent for evaporation of spirits in copper tanks, namely, 4 per cent the first year; 3 per cent the second year; 2 per cent the third year; 2 per cent the fourth year and 1 per cent per year from the fifth to the tenth year, which equals 17 per cent allowance for supposed shrinkage, but when the spirits are kept in wood, an allowance of 33 per cent is made for the same period of time. This conclusively proves that the evaporation or shrinkage is considerably more in wood than in copper tanks.
In Great Britain, whiskey must be kept for three years in oak or wooden casks before being released for home consumption, but the foreign distilleries in Great Britain, France, Holland or any other country can export their new, raw material, made yesterday, and that is the "rotgut" we frequently receive. It is true that a recent order in council requires that foreign spirits should be at least two years old, but where is the proof? And, moreover, the order in council does not state it must be aged in wood; certainly not the gin from Holland or England that arrives here as colourless as the day it came out of the still, whereas if it had been stored in wood it would have been straw or amber colour.
I would also draw attention, Mr. Speaker, to the many false representations on the bottles, flasks and other packages of goods coming into this country, and would advise the government to adopt the English law in that respect. No bottle of brandy can enter England without an official stamp stating that it is distilled from pure grape wine, and it is not surprising that England has on her bonded docks the finest wines and liquors in the world.
I have been familiar with the Customs and Excise department, now merged into one, for nearly half a century, and I have a very high appreciation of the standing of the deputy ministers and other officials in those departments. I am not speaking of the ministers themselves because they never remain long enough. To-day we Lave excellent officials, and I am sure they would welcome an order in council, providing that excise stamps, affixed to bottles, should show clearly whether the contents have been aged in wood or in copper tanks, with the date of bottling as well as age and strength. I have no doubt these gentlemen will assist me in making my suggestions more concete, so as to offer the gov-

Special War Revenue Act
eminent a bill that will be satisfactory to all concerned.
Let us build up the same reputation for our goods as they have done in Great Britain and, at the same time, increase our revenue. This would decrease bootlegging and moonshine stuff, as the people would insist upon having the article certified by the government, and would refuse the concoctions as we would refuse a counterfeit bank note.
With reference to recent smuggling of liquor into the United States via Canada, owing to prohibition in the United States,
I believe this could be remedied to the satisfaction of the English, American and Canadian governments. In this connection, liquor has been imported consigned to a bonded warehouse in Canada, then export papers have been obtained to tranship these good'

to St. Pierre and Miquelon, Mexico, Japan or the Sandwich islands. These goods, as has been clearly proven in the customs probe, never reach their supposed destination, but are landed in transit on the American side. This can easily be prevented by the Customs department, of which the hon. Mr. Boivin is now the vigilant head, by not allowing any transhipment of foreign liquors in bond after having been warehoused at any port of entry in the Dominion. Duty would then have to be paid upon such consignments and the government would derive a larger revenue.
It is easy to understand, Mr. Speaker, that no foreign shipper would consign goods to Montreal or Toronto if they were purchased by a legitimate dealer in New York, Chicago, New Orleans or San Francisco. This would not prevent shipment through Canada from the other side to another country', on a through bill of lading, and would therefore not deprive transportation companies of freight charges upon such shipments.
I will not dwell upon the question of wine at any length. I might say, however, that wine should never be classed with spirits. Spirits are distilled and wine is made from the natural fermentation of the grape. I would suggest, however, that no wine, either foreign or native, should be allowed to be sold if manufactured from dried raisins with sugar and alcohol added. The governments of Portugal, Spain. France and Germany have very strict regulations regarding the sale of wines for consumption in their countries. There is nothing more pleasant or healthful than pure wine with a lovely bouquet, developed only by the evaporation of ethers, and the combination of the natural spirit with the succinic, tartaric, tannic, citric and malic acids contained in the wine. The colouring is formed in the grape skin during its ripening, by the action of the sun and soil. But I will leave this to another occasion.
In conclusion I wish to assure my prohibition and temperance friends, if there are any in this House, that I have no desire to interfere with their opinions concerning the liquor traffic. I respect the views of every man on that question, but I would remind them, if they allow me, that liquor is absolutely necesary in certain cases. I might tell hon. members about a certain town in Nevada where they have the most stringent prohibition law ever enacted. One provision of the law is that no person can purchase a drop of liquor unless he has been bitten by a snake, and the certificate which he has to obtain from the medical practitioner of the town must be endorsed by the mayor and three aldermen. One day a traveller arrived at the hotel in the town and said, "'I must have a drop of brandy or I will die." The hotel man said: "You cannot get any liquor in this place unless you are bitten by a snake." Where are the snakes? "They are up in the mountain yonder." The poor man wended his way up the mountain with about a hundred pilgrims ahead of him, but when he reached the summit the snake was too tired and it refused to bite. It is a terrible thing to be deprived of liquor under those conditions. Only the other day a man was knocked unconscious at the corner of 42nd street and Fifth avenue, New York. He happened to have a flask in his hip pocket. On the way to the Bellevue hospital in the ambulance the poor man came to and he felt something trickling down his leg. He exclaimed: "Great Scott, I hope it's blood."
I have the honour which very few other hon. members have had of seeing Sir John A. Macdonald in this House as well as his successors. I was quite a young man, but we all liked Sir John and I think he liked me. I have seen all his successors, Sir John Thompson, Sir Charles Tupper, Sir Robert Borden, my right hon. friend, Mr. Meighen, and now my dear friend, Mr. Mackenzie King. I do not see any reason why I should not disclose this secret if it is a secret. I am sorry Hansard is here for part of my remarks. In 1896 I came to Ottawa and sat in the council chamber where I saw Mr. Fielding, Mr. Davies, Mr. Blair, Mr. Paterson, Sir Henry Joly de Lotbiniere and Mr. Sifton. I came with the very proposition that I am bringing before the House to-day and they thought well of it.
I have been an agent for distilleries for some years and I think a good deal of our

distillers. There are no better citizens than our distillers; but they have made millions and as I told some of the representatives of the distillers who are here to-day, I think that owing to our great war debt these gentlemen should give us a piece of the melon. I do not think it would be any hardship for them to agree that, outside of the changes I suggested, we should get a share of the profits. I do not know how that could be worked out, but it would be a good thing. As lion, members know, during the war there was a time of great uncertainty whether they should continue operations. There are hon. members who remember quite well when there was total prohibition and prevention of the manufacture of spirits in this country and there was a time when the distillers had cold feet. If they were to give this country a share of their profits we would be copartners in their business; there would be a better feeling throughout the country, and there would be for the distillers more stability, which should exist as it does in all other countries. Otherwise, if you raise the two year law that I referred to a few minutes ago, you might have many distilleries cropping up throughout Canada as has occurred in Scotland, France and other countries.
What limit would the hon. gentleman put upon their profits?

That is a
difficult question to answer. I do not know, but from what I know of the profits of the last fifty years which of course they have not on hand, but which have been handed down from father to son, I think they could give something. Hon. members know of the wealth of the large distilleries, such as the Corby's and the Seagram's. They certainly deserve it because they made better spirits than the American people did and they made a reputation in Canada for their product. They are valuable citizens; they give employment to large numbers of people and so on. This is a very delicate question because these gentlemen are good friends of mine; but I think they should do their share toward reducing our debt, and I am sure the leaders of the different parties in this House would look upon a project of that sort with some favour if there is still going to be distillation and sale.
In conclusion, let me refer to another source of revenue which I believe could be developed. I believe that our millionaire philanthropists in Canada should, while they are still living, do a little more than they ire doing for the welfare of their country

or their home cities or towns. Our Canadians are very charitable; in their wills they leave large amounts for hospitals and homes of different kinds. If they did that during their lifetime it would be more to their credit; they would see what they were doing, and it would help this country enormously. If a man who has an income of $200,000 or $300,000 a year gives $50,000 out of it, he is giving practically nothing if you take into consideration the income tax and the succession tax in Quebec. If a man is worth a million dollars he has to pay $60,000 in succession tax which the province gets. If while he is living he devotes some of his revenue to the public good he is doing something for the welfare of his country. Unfortunately, men who are wrapped up in business are not in the habit of handing out their money; they always think there is going to be a lean year or rainy day. It is only when they are dying that they see a different horizon and their outlook becomes broader. That is a question which these millionaires who are hoarding their capita! should consider.
I may not have the honour of being very long in this House and this may be my last utterance. I feel that I could be easily replaced by a man who could do more for the country. But before I resign I must take this occasion to thank all hon. members for their kindly attitude toward me and for making me feel at home and comfortable. If I leave the House I shall have great pleasure in saying how well I was received by my friends from Ontario and the eastern and western provinces who understood my particular temperament and were kind and charitable.
Before resuming my seat I wish to take the House into my confidence in connection with a little dream I had the other night. We dream here a good deal. I dreamed that I died in Ottawa. I thought I was a senator and consequently I thought I was dead. I dreamed that I had left $100,000 to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), $100,000 to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), and $100,000 to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rofob). It was stipulated in the will that they should each put into my coffin $1,000 to show that they had confidence in me and respected my word. This would prove that they believed I had the wherewithal to meet the provision of the will. Well, while lying there I saw the Prime Minister come along gaily and deposit $1,000 in fresh bills.

I was not here when vote 133 was under discussion. If the minister would be good enough to give me the information I should like to know what will be the probable cost of the new post office at Chipman. I am anxious to get some information also with regard to the post office at Moncton.

The item was
passed some days ago but I am glad to give the hon. gentleman the information. We are asking for $5,000 to complete the construction of the building at Chipman. A contract was entered into and out of the appropriation of $10,000 for 19215-26 $8,000 3 p.m. was spent, $7,500 being on the contract and $500 for the purchase of the site. An unexpended balance of $2,000 is being re-voted this year. The fixtures for the post office have been contracted for and are now being placed. For these fixtures six tenders were received, ranging from $945 to $1,576. The lowest tender of $945. from the Office Specialty Company, was accepted.
I am not so much concerned about the fixtures. What was the total cost of the structure including the site?
The contract was for $8,445.

What about the building at Moncton? For a good many years the people there have been asking for a post office. Business men, boards of trade and other public bodies have been requesting the government to put up a new post office at a point east of the subway so-called, and notwithstanding the preference as to location indicated by these people the government bought a very expensive site from one of its own friends, the McManus Company. For that site they paid $40,000. The property is still occupied by the McManus people at a rental of $10 a month. A site costing $40,000 is being rented to the original vendor or a member of the family at the handsome sum of $40 a month, and no move has yet been made by the government to build the post office. Is this delay due to the opposition that has developed from the business men of Moncton, and if so is it the intention to abandon the proposed site? What does the minister intend to do about the matter, and why has nothing been done so far towards erecting the building? I believe this is a political deal made to suit the purposes of a valiant supporter of the government. The price paid was excessive, being nearly double the amount of the assessed valuation of the site, which is wholly unsuitable from the standpoint of the business people of Moncton, and the whole transaction has a very unsavoury smell. We ought to know something about it.

I shall be glad to give my hon. friend full information on the subject. I absolutely resent his remarks. It is true that at the last session parliament did vote moneys for the purchase of a post office site in Moncton. Several sites were suggested. Those in the down-town section were carefully appraised as were also the proposed sites above the subway. The site my hon. friend speaks of was considered by the appraisers, by departmental officials and by myself-because I made an inspection- as the proper site for a post office building in Moncton. The price is a reasonable one and is confirmed by the assessors and by departmental officials. I am not prepared to say whether it suited the business community, but we had in mind other people than those with property to sell in the business section. We had petitions from people in the downtown section and from residents of Moncton, one for and one against the downtown location. If any gentlemen familiar with Moncton will, when arriving there by train, pass
Supply-Public Works

from the station across to the property owned by the government they will confirm my judgment and that of the officials of the department. This was a proper purchase and is an ideal spot for a public building in Moncton.

If that is so, why have not the government constructed the building? Is it because Moncton voted against the government on October 29 last? Why is the building rented for the absurd sum of $40 a month? That is not an adequate rental for a building costing over $40,000. I would like to tell the committee that this was a residential property not in the business district, although it is on a continuation of the main street. I venture to say that the preponderance of opinion as evidenced by public bodies, and not by individuals having private interests to serve, has been against this site from the very beginning. But this property was purchased from one of the members of the New Brunswick legislature who supported the late government there, and so far as I can observe that is the only reason for the purchase. I ask why the building has not been proceeded with.
The property was bought because it was the proper site for a public building. The price was fair, but the criticism of my hon. friend is not fair.

Would the minister tell
me why construction is not being proceeded with?
Yes. A large sum is required, and the matter is under consideration as to whether it is now opportune for us to proceed with the construction.

Am I right?

The amount is a little
over $90,000. Now, a federal building in a city like Calgary is almost essential. It should not be a post office building. There should be a post office on the ground floor, and provision should be made for every federal service-the land office, the immigration office, the railway commission, and others. A building of about eight storeys would cost approximately $1,500,000, or let us say $1,600,000. If a special form of security were issued to provide public works in this country, where the rental paid would be sufficient to meet the interest on the capital expenditure plus a sinking fund, it would be a very economical procedure. Now suppose we fixed the amount at $1,600,000 in the present case and paid

as high a rate as 5 per cent; that would be $80,000. But it would not be necessary to spend quite that much money, and the rate of interest would be less than 5 per cent. It would therefore follow that the interest could be paid, and a sufficient sum set aside for sinking fund sufficient to amortize the entire loan at the end of twenty years, and the country would own the building. I desire to urge upon the administration an appropriation for the purpose of enabling the building to be commenced, basing that appropriation upon the rentals now paid, so that there will be set up in the public records of this country an account for that particular building, and the rentals that are now being paid will be, without increase, credited to that account from year to year, being sufficient to liquidate the entire interest charges, with a sinking fund that will entirely absorb the loan within fifteen or twenty years. While I am speaking on that subject, I have the same observation to make with respect to the public buildings in this city. From time to time I have looked into the situation here. This country owns a large area of property west of the Supreme court buildings facing on the river. All those buildings belong to the crown, as I understand it. Let us assume it would cost $8,000,000 to put up a suitable departmental building covering that area. Some may say it would cost much more than that, but for the purposes of the services of this country we do not require the most ornate building in the world, and I am informed that the rent paid in this city b3' the government, notwithstanding that we have the new Hunter building, and notwithstanding the purchase of other buildings, amounts to nearly $700,000 per annum.

When we try to find the
total expenditure of any one department, we find estimates and expenditures scattered throughout the book under several different departments.

My query is why do they come under public works?
The Department of Public Works maintains all the public buildings.

We have charge of their construction, care and maintenance.

All I am saying is that when you look up the estimates of the Department of Agriculture you do not find there the items of expenditure on buildings.
No.
Would the minister give us the annual expenditure on buildings in connection with the experimental farm at Ottawa?

I quite understand the explanation, but due to this system it is very difficult to find out what the cost of any particular service is. For instance, on page 26 I find item No. 102, "construction of magazine, Halifax. 850,000," and "reconditioning mine sweeper, $50,000," the latter is a marine job, and various other items for construction. The same is true with regard to the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. You will find twenty different items scattered through this book chargeable to Agriculture which do not appear under Agriculture estimates, and you have to hunt the whole book through from end to end to find how much money is being expended on any particular service. That does not seem to me like business.

May I bring to the attention of the minister the representations of two or three groups of public employees? Right here in the city of Ottawa I am informed that the office cleaners, not in this building, but in the other offices, receive $1.25 daily for their morning's cleaning, or $32.50 a month. Not only is that a low item which they think Should be increased, but more than that, I am informed that if these women are absent one or two days owing to illness, pay is deducted. It seems to me that is a very small way, to say the least, of dealing with these lower paid employees, and I hope the minister will see his way to remedy that state of affairs.
There is another group that has made representations to me, and that is the elevator operators in these various public buildings in the city of Ottawa. They state that there are now five classes of salaries for elevatoi operators under the new classification, and yet all the employees are performing the same kind of wo-rk. For example, right here in the House of Commons and in the Senate there are seven elevators operating during the session, and four operators get a maximum salary of S1.260, one a maximum of $1,200, two a maximum of $1,080, and one operator, who is single, a maximum of $960. All are performing the same class of work and all are permanent employees. I am sure these representations have been made to the minister, and I would ask if there is not a possibility of having the matter satisfactorily adjusted Then there is this further fact: I am informed that those employed by the House of Commons and those employed by the Senate are receiving different wages for the same class of work. This, of course, leads to considerable heart-burning and creates a feeling that the lower paid employees are not receiving fair play.

Which class is the
highest paid?

The Senate employees. It would seem to me that as we are trying to consolidate our departments in one building, or a series of buildings, we might

Supply-Public Works
very well undertake to consolidate the departments themselves and the different types of work. We have heard about the duplication in connection with our railway systems. We have absolutely unwarranted duplication right under our noses every day. I cannot for the life of me see why a staff under one management cannot manage the affairs of these buildings, whether it is in the eastern part of this structure, or in the House of Commons portion. We have two sets of doormen, two sets of charwomen, two sets of cleaners, two post offices with separate staffs, and the same thing all down the line, and why this should be passes my comprehension. It seems to me that if these matters were managed in a businesslike way there would be a consolidation of these departments under one management. May I say in closing that I should like to get answers from the minister to the questions I put with regard to these various classes of lower paid employees.

The char service is largely carried on by female help. The work is done early in the morning and occupies about two and a half hours, paid for at the rate of $1.25 per day. That is not a bad wage for the time occupied, which is not very great each day. The department, I think, have found that the char service is being done efficiently, and although those engaged in it would welcome a larger amount of remuneration, still it is considered that $1.2& for two and a half hours' work a day is probably as much as the government would be entitled to pay. Now in regard to the elevator and other services-[DOT]
Before the minister leaves that subject, may I suggest to him that provision should be made for fairer treatment of these employees in the matter of sick leave and questions of that kind?

These employees are not regarded as part of the civil service. They are paid at what is known as " prevailing rates " and have not been considered in the light of civil servants. There is something in what my hon. friend has suggested with respect to sick leave. I may point out, however, that it is a pretty difficult service to control, and one that requires careful supervision:	Representations have been made on
this subject and they will be given consideration. The employees in the House of Commons, I believe, enjoy certain holidays and other privileges that are not enjoyed in other branches of the service.
With respect to the elevator operators there is a difference in the matter of annual increase of pay. There are also temporary employees who have not been made permanent. The latter class are not given an annual increase and probably have not been fairfy treated in that regard. I am asking that these temporary employees, some of whom have been in the service for twenty years, should be made permanent. I think they should be brought in and placed on a footing of equality with other employees.
That is a matter for the government to do. It is a wonder they have not already done it.

The item of $385,000 for char service in the departments generally, including the payment of $100' for firing the noon gun, is a pretty large amount. There must be a lot of women employed if the rate of pay for the char service is only $1.25 a day.

Would any
hon. member suggest that the elevator men in the Senate enjoy a better rate of pay because they have to exercise greater care over those who use the elevators?

Yes, the regular employees.

Some are permanent employees, and others are temporary employees.
What is the total number of employees in the char service and the amount paid in salaries each year?

The bonus is cut out
altogether.

How many
elevator attendants are there including those in the Senate?

There are 16
elevator attendants employed during the session.

There is an item
here which requires explanation. It is that of $100 for firing the noon gun. I thought this government boasted of its economy. If so it should cut out all this noon gun firing. Is there any special necessity for having this gun fired at Ottawa? Perhaps it is the hour of the cabinet meeting, or it may have some other special significance. Is the man who fires the gun an artillery man, or what is the special reason for carrying on this practice when it has been cut out in all other parts of Canada?

It is an old
practice, it costs $100 a year, and I observe that when the gun goes off nearly every member of the House takes out his watch to see the time. I think it would be a mistake to dispense with it.
Why is this piece of antiquity continued in Ottawa when it has been abolished in all other cities?
Not all.

It is supposed to
be. They do not employ a man to fire the gun any other place. Have the people in Ottawa a bad set of watches?

I think they
should be checked anyway, so that they could get the right time once a day.

If you cut out the noon gun in Ottawa you upset the whole timing system of the city. Every house is run on the noon gun. At every gathering in the city when the gun is fired, everyone pulls out his watch and sets it. It is historical. It goes back to the days of Colonel By when Parliament Hill was then Barracks Hill. When visitors and tourists are being shown around the beautiful Parliament grounds and build-

ings and the gun suddenly goes off the guide is able to tell them a wonderful story. He can draw on his imagination and suggest that the gun is now fired from a spot where the Indians camped in the early days. We could not do without our noon gun.
Mr. RO'SS (Kingston):	This is not the
explanation. This practice has been discontinued in other cities for the sake of economy.
This is the capital of the Dominion.

Is it maintained
because it is the capital. Is the whole city run by the noon day gun?

I understood the minister to say a moment ago that the increase of $10,000 in the item of lighting for Dominion public buildings was partly due to the fact that ithe Department of Public Works was now paying for the lighting of the Canadian building in London.

Under the Public Works Act it is under the Department of Public Works just as other buildings are. We are asking for supply in order that we may heat, light and take care of the building generally through the commissioner.

Does the Department of Public Works pay everything in connection with that building as it would with regard to a building in Ottawa, that is, the taxes, ground rent, lighting, heating, char service and everything of that kind?
Yes, through the commissioner in London.	*
Is that not a new venture?
Yes.

I do not think that was the policy when I was there. I quite admit we had not as good a building as the present one, but I think all the charges in connection with it were paid out of the High Commissioner's vote.

Of course at that time the hon. member was in a rented building and the department had not any direct interest in the commissioner's office. But since the property now known as the Canadian building was taken over and reconstructed, the Department of Public Works came on the scene and we are now asking parliament to vote supply for maintenance of that building.

Is this the first
year?

The first regular
year that has been in operation.

It is then rather a good time to suggest that the hon. gentleman is not responsible for one cent being spent there. He has not the slightest supervision of expenditure. He has nothing to do with the charwomen or anything else there. He neither hires nor fires the man that looks after the furnace or anything else. They are all employees of the local office.
The Civil Service Commission hire and fire.
In England?

Yes.
Supply-Public Works

It seems to me that the goverijment sometimes strain at gnats and swallow camels. They are making a great deal out of a gnat in this case. I have a shrewd suspicion that the real reason they are doing that is that it is not convenient to show the annual carrying cost of that building in an item of $110,000 a year. There is so much trouble about this gnat. My hon. friend is put into this position that he is asking for a vote for something which he knows nothing about and which his officers iknow nothing about. If a man is to be hired to look after the furnace in the Canadian building in London, how is he appointed by the 'Civil Service Commission?
Firemen are exempt under the Civil Service Act.

I knew they
were. That was the reason I was taking my hon. friend at his word for the moment, because when I was asking how the man was hired or fired I was told that it was done by the Civil Service Commission. I knew that was nonsense. What appointments have been made by the Civil Service Commission to positions in connection with the London office?

What I have said is right. We submit the list to the Civil Service Commission. Although they do not appoint the firemen, they indicate the position and the salary. Others on the staff are appointed by the commission. Of course our connection with the building is that merely of the Department of Public Works which is maintaining buildings say in Vancouver, and there is no reason why it should not maintain a building at London under the same conditions. We have our agent there, the High Commissioner, and the department is kept informed. There is nothing cumbersome, nothing unusual about this; indeed I think it is a proper procedure that the vote should come before parliament in this way.

The minister
now says that the Civil Service Commission apparently makes out the classification of services there. I want to know what appointments it has made there.
I have not a list at hand, but the salaries for caretakers, engineers and firemen which we provide for amount to $7,617.

That is exactly what I did not ask my hon. friend. He is fond of giving information that is not asked IMr. J. H. King.]
for. He gave information as to appointments being made by the Civil Service Commission. Now I ask him what appointments have been made to the London office by the Civil Service Commission.
I am informed that the Civil Service Commission approved all the caretakers, engineers and firemen employed in the Canadian building, London.
The whole thing comes down to this, that the High Commissioner over there makes the appointments and they are approved by the Civil Service Commission.
It comes down to that.
Who is my hon. friend's representative in England?
The High Commissioner.
We are learning something all the time. We learn now that the Hon. P. C. Larkin, the High Commissioner, is the representative of the Minister of Public Works in London.

My hon. friend
is unfair; he knows he is not speaking according to the book. The Hon. P. C. Larkin is High Commissioner for Canada in London, and in that position in addition to his other duties he represents the government of Canada in the administration of the Canadian building in London.
My hon. friend said that he had a representative over there and could run that office just as well as he could run an office in Vancouver.
Why exaggerate?
That is what my hon. friend said. He wants now to deny that. He did not say that he had his representative there and could run that office just as well as he could run a building in Vancouver?
My hon. friend is exaggerating.
My hon. friend's memory is as weak as his logic. I asked him who his representative was and he said it was the Canadian High Commissioner. It seems that is a farce.

It seems to me
it is a mistake for the Department of Public Works to take over this service. The High

Private Bills
Commissioner in London and his secretary are really the ones who administer the building, who pick out the men who are to do the work, and the charges for it should be through the High Commissioner's office. It is not reasonable to have the expenses over there divided into a number of departments so that it is impossible for anybody to find out the total cost of the building and the services in London. It is only camouflage to put it through the Department of Public Works when the High Commissioner and his office are responsible for the whole expenditure and are the people who really select the men. The minister has made a mistake in including this vote in his estimates. What is the total cost of the services in London?
Does that include ground rent?

It includes taxes, insurance, repairs, heating, lighting, power, rents, salaries of caretakers, engineers, and firemen. I do not think there is any option in the matter unless we amend the Public Works Act. There is no use creating any mystery about it. Mr. Larkin is in London and is surrounded by a capable staff, and as we approach the period of estimate-making we are advised as to how much their requirements will be. And that is entered in the Public Works estimates. One or two hon. gentlemen have made the same complaint about some items which in their opinion should properly come under the estimates of other departments to which they appertain. This has been pointed out in the case of Agriculture, for example. But the fact is that under the Public Works Act this department is responsible for the expenditures so included. There is no desire on my part to control expenditures that do not rightly come under my department, but this is the system which has been adopted.

How is it that from the time we have had a High Commissioner in London until to-day these services have not been administered by the Public Works department? It is true that we had a rented building, but we have throughout the country many such buildings which the Public Works department administers. If it is contrary to the act, how is it that until to-day the Public Works Department has not administered the services in London?
The High Commissioner is free to rent any buildings, but the moment a building becomes the property of the crown it comes under the Public Works department.
But the Public Works department has already administered rented buildings.

We have a grant for $1,400,000 for rented buildings occupied by other departments. Will the minister give us a list of those buildings, including the offices in Ottawa, for which rents are paid.

Would
the minister tell me whether it is true that officials and employees of the Interior department are distributed over twenty buildings in this city, or if not, how many?

The Department of the Interior, which includes the Indian department and the various branches, are in twelve different buildings in this city.
Supply-Public Works

I was informed by a man who ought to know that they had offices in twenty-six buildings. Even twelve buildings seem an enormous number for one department to be spread over. Is there any way whereby a more economical adjustment of that department could be brought about?

I think the way to accomplish that is by consolidation in new buildings. We were discussing that question this afternoon. The Parks branch of the department is a distinct branch and it is in its own quarters. The Indian department have their own quarters and so on through the department. The main offices of the department are in the Langevin block.

I would like to
ask the minister about the Carling building on Rank street between Sparks and Queen. When was the lease with Mr. Carling cancelled?

There was no
cancellation. The lease expired some months ago. I have not the exact date under my hand, but I shall be glad to supply my hon. friend with that information.

I understand Mr. Carling's lease expired and the building was left on the market empty. It was a very expensive building; I believe he had it on the market at $200,000 and he could not rent it to the government. I do not know why they left it. It had been occupied by the Department of the Interior from the time it was built. I understand that nothing Mr. Carling could do would induce the government to re-lease it. It was eventually sold to the President of the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association and I believe within twenty-four hours of the sale being effected a new lease was made out to that gentleman and his friends. That is the information I get. I do not know whether it was because Mr Carling was a son of his father, a former Conservative Minister of Agriculture, or not, but I know that building was lying idle for about a year. I understand the department have rented it and paid rent since last May although it was occupied only about a month or two months ago. The tenants who went into that building were removed from the Bryson building on Queen street, a building with light on four sides, to a building that has light just on Bank street. The building on Queen street was owned by the George Bryson Realty Company and it is now lying idle, while the building that the government could not use prior to the time that the

President of the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association bought it is now occupied by the Parks branch that was formerly in the Brj'-son building on Queen street.

My hon. friend is not correctly informed. The lease of the Carling building expired. There were changes and removals in the department. As my hon. friend living in Ottawa knows these things take place from time to time. It is true that a department has gone into that building, but it has been renovated and improved so that it is a satisfactory building to-day.

Is the Bryson
building on Queen street not satisfactory? It had been occupied by the Parks branch ever since it was built fifteen years ago. It is right behind the Hunter building with light on four sides; it is an isolated fireproof building. I know the property on Bank street. Up to the two top storeys it has light only front and back. The rest looks on to an alleyway; if they need light they get it from the alleyway. This building was occupied for a number of years. Mr. Carling lost on that transaction probably $100,000. The building was put on the market with the brokers at $200,000; then the price was reduced to $175,000, and finally when the building was lying there idle without rental he had to take the best offer he could get, which was $110,000 or $115,000. Therefore through the fact of the building not being occupied, he lost the difference between $110,000 or $115,000 and the $175,000 or $200,000 at which the building was put on the market. This looks to me like a clear case of patronage. We people in Ottawa do not like patronage at all; we are very much surprised that the Minister of Public Works would think of such a thing when ML Carling, who was a very prominent citizen, put up this building, thus helping to make Bank street the wonderful street that it is, the building lay empty for about a year on account of its not being well lighted; yet as soon as it becomes the property of the president of the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association it has plenty of light around it and becomes rented.

When the lease of that building expired and the department felt that it required certain alterations, did the minister give the lessor an opportunity of making those alterations? Did he make any requirement or suggestion to the lessor that the building would be suitable if certain alterations were made?

Supply-Public Works

My hon. friend
would understand the situation better if he would go over the numerous leases we have in Ottawa and if he realized the difficulty of accommodating various departments. A department is very much like the ordinary tenant who moves into a house and occupies it. After he is there a little while he finds the light not good or the premises dirty or cold, in the case of premises rented for departments the Department of Public Works hears of these things. We act as agents for the various departments and changes are made from time to time. When a man or a firm rents a building to the Department of Public Works or the government of Canada there is no assurance and no reason to have assurance of tenure any more than in the case of any other lessee. It is true that if departments are comfortably situated and complaints do not come in we try to continue the tenure, but changes will and do take place from time to time.

I quite appreciate the fact
that the lessor of a building to the government has no right to expect from the government more than from any other lessee. But I think he has a righ't to expect that if his lessee, the government, has any fault to find with the premises, he might be informed and given an opportunity of making the necessary alterations. It strikes me as a new member of this House as rather strange, to say the least, that when the premises had been vacated by the government on the expiration of the lease the new Liberal owner is given an opportunity of putting the building into condition, meeting the requirements of the department and becoming himself a lessor. Any lessee who has occupied as a tenant premises for any considerable time usually, if he finds fault with the premises, gives his lessor an opportunity of putting them into proper condition.

As the result of certain reorganization in the last two or three years a number of changes were necessitated in the Immigration department, and these changes are all justified. The reference to the president of the East Ottawa Liberal Association is without point.

The minister
means the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association. Did the department make any extensive repairs to that building or was the work all done by the owners?
Largely by the owners.

Ordinary men on the street inform me that they have seen
Public Works men around the building during the past six months. What was wrong with the Bryson building? That building has been occupied by the Parks branch alone. It is an isolated building with light on four sides and it seems rather strange that it should be vacated and the Parks branch transferred to a building which has been condemned for want of light.
The Parks branch complained that there was not sufficient accommodation and that the building was cold and dirty. They wanted to be transferred.
Was the Journal building vacated for the same reason? Was it, too, cold and dirty simply because it happened to be the Journal building?
I suppose the hon. gentleman would wish the government to continue renting the Journal building. Our lease expired and we moved.

Reverting to the Carling building, did the department comunicate with the owner before he made the improvements? Did they submit to him certain specifications for improvements and request him to comply with them?
We insisted upon the improvements being made before the building was leased.

Might not the department
have done precisely the same thing with the previous owner?
He was not given an opportunity.

Exactly; Mr. Carling was not given an opportunity. Aparently what the government could do for the one man they could not do for the other. They could not go to the old lessor, whose tenants they had been for years, and tell him that the building as it stood was not suitable and demand certain improvements and alterations. They ' could not do that in his case but they could with the next owner who happens to be a Liberal.

It would be ridiculous to suggest that Mr. Gordon Edwards, a member of a family that has been a milch cow to the Liberal party for a quarter of a century, would not be given an opportunity in this matter.

The hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) evidently did not hear me say that there was a reorganization. We moved from the Norlite building to the Jackson building for consolidation pur-
Supply-Public Works

poses in connection with the Immigration department. That was at the request of the minister. We then consolidated the Lands branch in the Norlite building, removing a part of that branch from the Carling building. That is how the Carling building was vacated in the first place. On the occasion of a further reorganization the Parks branch at their request were transferred from the Bryson building to the Carling building.
What are the rentals respectively of the two buildings?

I have not the information here; the transaction took place some months ago. But the rentals, I fancy, are about the same. I shall look into the question. In the Carling building we found increased accommodation for the Parks branch, and naturally as therq' was more space the rent would be higher. -

The minister has not yet satisfactorily answered me. I am prepared to accept the statement that there had to be a reorganization of certain branches. After that reorganization the plans of the government evidently fit into the Carling building.
My question is this: could not 9 p.m. those plans have fitted into the Carling building while it was owned by the other gentlemen? Do they fit in now better than they did before, merely because the present owner is a Liberal and a friend and supporter of the government? Could not the same improvements and changes, the same structural alterations, have been effected under the old lessor as under the new?

During and after the consolidation the Carling building was vacant for a period of nearly one and a half years. We had left it and we went back to it at the request of the Parks branch, which needed better and larger quarters.
- Mr. BURY: That does not answer my point.

I presume we may discuss under this item the famous Union Club purchase. How much has been spent on this building for furnishings and so forth since the close of the fiscal year which is covered by the last report of the Auditor General, that is to say, since March 31, 1925?

I have not the capital expenditure; I gave that to the House last year. The information I gave to-day has reference to the vote, now under consideration, for maintenance. I submitted the details this afternoon. The total is $35,110.73.
[Mr. J. H. King.l
I am not interested in the maintenance. I want to know what we have spent on the structure in addition to the cost.
There is a total expenditure of $1,540,781.
We have spent a considerable sum in refurbishing and refurnishing the building since buying it.

In addition to the purchase price a certain amount of reconstruction was necessary. That information was given last year, together with the amount for furnishings. I have not the information here as to those expenditures; I have the explanation of the expenditure for the coming year.
That is for maintenance.
Yes.
Is there any expenditure contemplated for further furnishings in the coming year?
No.

So we may take it for
granted that the building has cost the country as it now stands $1,500,000?
Yes.
Right here.
Do they approve of this?
We do not approve of twisting it.

I am reading absolutely
from the record.
Has the record been changed?

No, the record has not
been changed. I will continue with the items. A settee $279.84f; a satinwood table $803; a walnut table $187.80; two chairs $184.93'; a pair of corner cabinets $180.07; nineteen fenders $155,73; sundries $255.75. Then there was furniture purchased in Canada to the value of $9,800, including $2,200 to the Andrew Malcolm Company. That is a total of $19,424.63 for furniture up to that time, when the building had not been completed, and since that time over a quarter of a million dollars more has been spent, if I understood the figures correctly from the minister. That makes a total of $1,540,000, less $1,302,421.88 up to March 31, 1925. I would like to ask if there is any justification for this extravagance.
Will the minister give the comparison between what was paid in that case for the leasehold interest and what the amount was in the case of Canada?
I am speaking of the ground lease.

I am aware of that, but you
paid something for the lessee's interest in that lease.
Yes, but-

done 'by Messrs. Trollope & Colls, Limited, the foremost and most reliable contractors in London. They in competition with other contractors submitted prices as to what the work would be done for. Their price was accepted, and I am satisfied that if hon. gentle-mep have an opportunity of visiting London and seeing this building they will not complain very much in regard to Canada's investment.

May I ask the hon. minister
now to answer what was the most material question in that comparison? One government has a lease for a certain number of years at a certain rental of a certain area. It had to buy the lessee's interest in that lease, and the smaller the rent, the longer the term, and the better the terms of the renewal lease, the bigger the price it will pay. That is perfectly obvious. I want to know if the minister is going to give this House a proper comparison between the bargain made by this Dominion, and that made by South Africa, or by any other country for its leasehold interest. What was paid for the leasehold interest in each case?

The minister can give
the committee, if he will just refer to his figures, what we paid for the lease. I know the property. I saw it when the front was all torn out of the building, and the new front was being built in. If the minister will give us the amount we paid for the lease-which for the moment I have forgotten, but it runs into a very large sum- and then tell us what it cost to remodel the face of the building-because they took out the old face of the building, leaving very little else-that will give us some idea. The minister speaks about the ground area. Unfortunately that building is a very shallow one. While its general location is excellent, I admit, as everybody must admit who is familiar with the Trafalgar Square district, although the side of the street the Union Club is on is not as much travelled, I think, as the side immediately opposite, yet the location is not so super-excellent as the minister would lead us to believe. But I am not going to quibble over that. It is a good location. but, as I say, the building is a very shallow one. It is a sort of triangular affair, on an obtuse corner, and the whole front of the building had to be torn out and rebuilt with a stone front, with the result that it looks very well.

The minister mentioned a moment ago a building that undoubtedly ought to have been secured, Cox's Bank on Waterloo Place. It is a perfectly new building, modern in every respect, a magnificent building with 114,000 square feet of space. The minister gave the ground area as 10,000 square feet, as compared with 9,000 feet in the other building, but the Cox building is a magnificent one, a modern stone building ideally located, facing directly across to Whitehall. It is ideally located for the purpose of a Dominion government in London, a much better location than the site on Trafalgar Square. I admit that for retail business perhaps, the sale of tickets, for instance, the particular section where the present building stands is very good. It is largely occupied now by offices of various steamship companies; the Canadian Pacific is almost across the Street, and there are the Grand Hotel and other buildings. As a location for business I admit it is better than Waterloo Place where Cox's Bank is, but for an office building for Dominion government purposes the Cox's Bank location, to my mind, would have been very much better. Furthermore, you would have had four or five times the floor space that this building supplies. The government could then have rented part of the building, but as we are situated at the present time in London, the building is more than fully occupied and does not house all the government services.
Practically all.
Almost all, but not quite.

There is space
there to spare.

II think the minister will find that you cannot put the government services now in London in that building. I was fully advised of that a year or so ago when I was over there. But I am not complaining that the location is not a good one. That is not the question. The question is, are we getting for the expenditure we put into that building the best return? I submit that we are not. I think the government made a serious mistake when it did not secure Cox's building for this purpose, which in my opinion is the best location for the purpose in London. The Australian building, which is further down towards the city, is a much better place for the headquarters for the Agent General and for Dominion government purposes than is the Union Club building which we purchased. It is too late to quibble over the matter now, I suppose, but I want to recall to the attention of the minister and of the

Supply-Public Works
committee that before this deal was consummated I brought the matter to the attention of the House in 1923, indeed in 1922, before the Prime Minister went to England, and he stood in his place in the House and promised us that the matter would not be consummated until it had been further discussed by parliament. But in the interim we were committed to this purchase by a certain Colonel Hyde, if I remember rightly. Again, in 1923 we warned the government that it was not making the best possible bargain. Now I think when we have all the expenditures before us it will be found that we have bought a very costly location which gives us not by any means the best possible accommodation for our Canadian services.
I would ask the minister to give us separately the cost of the purchase of the lease, the cost of renovating and rebuilding the structure, and the cost of the furnishings to date.

Is that the complete cost
of reconstruction?
Yes, if I remember rightly. The hon. member for York-Sun-bury gave the cost of the furnishings a moment ago.

Only up to March 31st
of last year.

As a matter of fact it
would amount to about $1,500,000 for the lease and the rebuilding of the structure.
The total capital expenditure to date is $1,540,000.

We would like to get from the minister his defence of the purchase. I am not going to question the location for I am not able to speak as to that, and there is a difference of opinion. But we will concede that the location is a good one. We should know the purchase price of the lease before we can understand exactly the comparisons made by the minister with the locations of the buildings of other dominions.

I think I gave
that information very concisely this afternoon, but I will read it again: London, Canadian building: Paid for equipment of the Union
Club, interest in site and building, including adjustment of taxes and costs of transfer and registration, $1,009,436.74. I think that is the information my hon. friend wants. Then the amount for the reconstruction and improvement of the building is $531,344.81. I deem it best to give the figures in dollars and cents rather than in pounds. The total capital expenditure is $1,541,781.

If I understood the
minister, this building cost approximately $1,000,000; $500,000 was expended upon reconstruction and improvement, and we have to give it up in thirty years?

No, we do not.
We have the option of continuing.
What is the increase in the rental?

Who authorized the
extravagant furnishings for this building?

I do not think
the furnishings are extravagant; I think they are in keeping with the building and the location. The money for this purpose was voted at the last session of parliament.

Does the minister
justify it?
Yes, entirely.
On what ground?
As being necessary for a building so situated.

What did South Africa pay
for its lease?

I have not that
information.

Then it is impossible to make a comparison. It is utterly futile to compare a lease with a rental of two thousand a year with another lease with a rental of two thousand a year unless one knows what was paid for the leasehold interest in each case.

What is the cost
of furnishing the building up to the present time?

I do not happen
to have that information at hand at present. The hon. member for York-Sunbury gave from the Auditor General's report a few moments ago the expenditure for furnishings for the building. I have already given the total capital expenditure, and we are dealing
Supply-Public Works

now with the item for maintenance for the coming year. I shall be glad to give to my hon. friend the information he asks for, but I regret that I do not happen to have it here just now.

The amount as shown by the Auditor General's report was a little less than 125,000. Since the date of that expenditure the building has been completely furnished and the total amount must be greatly in excess of the sum mentioned. I should like to have that information if I could get it in some detail.

I shall be very
glad to bring down a return containing the information.
In addition to the offices mentioned by the minister, what other offices are accommodated in this building?

I am advised
that the government agencies and offices in London are now housed within the Canadian building. There may be one or two offices maintained down town for the convenience of the public, but the headquarters of the offices in London are now within the Canadian building.	That was true when I was in
London this year and it certainly was the intention of the High Commissioner to have that done.

What offices are
maintained downtown?

I do not know of any, with this exception:	The Immigration
department have offices scattered throughout England. They may find it necessary to maintain a sub-agency down town away from the main office in the Canadian building. The same is true of the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Soldiers Pension branch, and other departments.

And the National Railways.
*

The National
Railways are a separate corporation. They have their own office across the street from the Canadian building.
Would the minister tell us something about these two book cases which cost $1,900?
They are very beautiful bookcases and are good value for the money. If hon. members saw the furniture they would be well satisfied in regard to the outlay.
Tell us something about it.
I would rather my hon. friend would get a magazine and read about it.
Go over there and see it for yourself.
I was over there.
The item for rents has increased from $1,410,000 to $1,440,000. What is the explanation of that increase?

I gave that information to the committee a little while ago.
, Included in the increase are the following items: London, England, Canadian building, $9,733; Duford building and McDougald building, Ottawa, occupied by the Department of Marine and the Department of Mounted Police, $14,458; Blythe building, occupied by the Mines department, $3,600; premises at 31 Sparks street, occupied by the Post Office Department, $900, making a total of $28,691.
When the minister brings down a return of the expenditure incurred in furnishing this building, will he include a list of the offices in the building and a list of the offices maintained outside?
In London? Yes.
I notice a very substantial increase in the item for the salaries of caretakers, engineers, and so forth. How does the minister account for that increase?

The explanation is the same as the one I gave this afternoon in regard to other items. Previous to last year these men received a bonus which was not voted in connection with the departmental estimates but was paid separately. Last year there was an adjustment of salaries, and as a result the bonus has been done away with. The increase here is largely accounted for by the adjustment in salaries.
It is a pretty large amount.
It really is not an addition. They received an augmentation before in the shape of a bonus, but it did not appear in this item. Now, by reason of the adjusted salaries, it does appear there.

I notice an item of $60,000 for the maintenance of Rideau Hall and grounds, improvements, furniture, and so

Supply-Public Works
forth. Will the minister give an explanation of this item so that we may all understand it? What has been the total cost of Rideau Hall up to date?

For the last ten
